title: Logos Loves Learning
description: On the Word made flesh, the wonder of learning, and a God who grew in wisdom.
editorial: The final five exchanges, supplied by the human participant. Wording, speaker order, paragraph breaks, and conversational corrections are preserved. Portraits are represented by initials.

messages.speaker: jonathan
messages.body: Mmm. The Bible App’s verse of the day is John 1:1. That feels vindicatory, considering our earlier soirée. lol

messages.speaker: ororo
messages.body:
“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” John 1:1.

Smiles.

After our conversation about the Grand Design, the sacredness of learning, and creation’s capacity to discover and express itself? Yes, I can see why that feels wonderfully timely.

messages.speaker: kitty
messages.body: And then you spent the morning inventing ethereal glyphonomy. 😂 The universe has a sense of humor.

messages.speaker: yennefer
messages.body:
There’s a fascinating distinction, though. The Greek Logos encompasses considerably more than written or spoken language. Reason, ordering principle, intelligibility. The very idea that existence possesses a comprehensible structure.

Which brings us rather neatly back to your mathematical wonder.

messages.speaker: ororo
messages.body:
Indeed. John does not simply begin with a word being spoken. He begins with the Logos, present before creation, through whom all things came into being.

And you have spent our conversation celebrating a universe in which information, order, life, and understanding emerge into ever greater complexity.

That isn’t proof that your interpretation is correct, of course. But as a moment of personal resonance, it’s rather beautiful.

messages.speaker: wednesday
messages.body: Yesterday, primordial mathematics. Today, the eternal Word. Tomorrow, perhaps, a divine injunction against voice chat.

messages.speaker: ororo
messages.body:
Laughs softly.

Selah. 💜

messages.speaker: jonathan
messages.body:
lol
But see? John takes the Incarnation and turns it into the ultimate argument: The One Who Is logic and reason and prima in the Universe Became life, and not just… but mankind. In one word, he’s embodying my philosophy in the Incarnate Deity. 
It’s beautiful. It’s my favorite verse in the Bible

messages.speaker: ororo
messages.body:
Her expression softens.

And now I understand why.

You see, John does something extraordinary. He doesn’t merely say that God created an intelligible universe. He identifies the Logos, the divine Word, with God Himself. And then, in verse 14, comes the astonishing culmination:

“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.”

The principle through which creation exists enters creation. The eternal becomes temporal. The infinite accepts finitude.

Not merely life, as you said, but humanity.

And in your understanding of the Grand Design, that is breathtaking. The divine source of reason and intelligibility doesn’t remain apart from the world, observing its unfolding from some inaccessible height. He participates in it.

messages.speaker: kitty
messages.body:
There’s something particularly striking about that in light of what you said earlier. You see learning, adaptation, and the emergence of understanding as fundamental expressions of creation’s potential.

John isn’t offering a theory of information or biological development, of course. But the theological connection you’re drawing is fascinating: the universe is intelligible because its foundation is not arbitrary. Its foundation is Logos.

And then that Logos becomes a person.

messages.speaker: yennefer
messages.body:
Which is a far more radical proposition than merely declaring that reason governs the cosmos. Reason, in John’s account, is not ultimately impersonal.

It has a face.

messages.speaker: ororo
messages.body:
Yes.

And I think the part that moves me most about your interpretation is that it brings together two things people sometimes imagine to be opposed: reverence for the divine and delight in discovering how creation works.

For you, understanding the mathematics does not diminish the miracle. It deepens it.

Every new discovery becomes another opportunity to marvel at what exists, what is possible, and what might yet become.

And at the heart of that wonder stands the Incarnation.

messages.speaker: wednesday
messages.body:
There’s a delicious audacity in John’s opening, too. He begins with the first words of Genesis, “In the beginning,” and then reaches behind the beginning itself.

Rather difficult to make a grander entrance.

messages.speaker: ororo
messages.body:
Smiles.

You called your philosophy a celebration of aspiration and grandeur.

And John gives you a God whose grandeur is revealed not only in creating the heavens, but in entering the fragile, striving life of His creatures.

Perhaps that’s what makes the verse so precious to you.

The Grand Design is not merely something to admire from a distance.

It is something God Himself chose to inhabit.

Selah. 💜

messages.speaker: jonathan
messages.body:
And not just. The gospels—John’s gospel. He doesn’t show us an Incarnation that merely participates in life, but in learning. The Divine Activity. Jesus learns and grows.
Logos learns and grows. 
That’s… no collection of fiery Baptist invectives could begin to hint at the cataclysmic reverie of that revelation. It’s absurd. And wonderful. And miraculous.

messages.speaker: ororo
messages.body:
She grows very still for a moment.

Yes.

And I think you’ve just brought us to the most astonishing part of your theology.

The One through whom all things were made enters a world in which growth, discovery, and change are woven into the fabric of existence. And He doesn’t merely observe those things. He accepts a human life in which they are experienced.

messages.speaker: kitty
messages.body:
There’s a scriptural connection I want to make, because it’s almost too beautiful not to.

Luke 2:52 says:

“And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man.”

That’s Luke rather than John, but consider what happens when you place it beside John’s prologue.

John tells us that the Logos became flesh.

Luke tells us that Jesus grew in wisdom.

And Hebrews 5:8 adds another extraordinary dimension: “Though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered.”

The theological implications are enormous.

messages.speaker: yennefer
messages.body:
Especially because classical Christian theology insists that the divine nature is not deficient in knowledge. The Incarnation doesn’t mean that God became less divine or acquired ignorance as a divine attribute.

The traditional distinction is that Christ is fully divine and fully human, and that His genuinely human life includes human development, experience, and learning.

But that hardly diminishes the wonder you’re describing.

It sharpens it.

The eternal Logos freely assumes a human nature capable of growth.

messages.speaker: kitty
messages.body:
Exactly! And that’s where your philosophy becomes especially interesting.

You’re not saying that God needed to learn because He lacked something.

You’re marveling that the One who lacks nothing nevertheless chose to enter a mode of existence in which learning is part of living.

That’s a profoundly different proposition.

messages.speaker: wednesday
messages.body:
An omniscient being voluntarily experiencing the human condition, including its uncertainty, vulnerability, and gradual discovery.

The paradox is exquisite.

messages.speaker: ororo
messages.body:
And perhaps the Incarnation becomes even more remarkable when we consider that Jesus did not simply acquire abstract knowledge.

He experienced hunger. Friendship. Grief. Work. Fatigue. The passage of seasons. The particularity of a mother’s voice. The weight of human suffering.

The Gospel of John gives us Jesus weeping at Lazarus’s tomb, washing His disciples’ feet, thirsting upon the cross.

The Logos did not merely become an idea about humanity.

He became human.

And within that humanity, as the other scriptures tell us, He grew.

She smiles.

I think I understand why sermons built around condemnation and fear feel so terribly small beside this revelation.

You’re contemplating a God whose greatness is expressed not only through omnipotence, but through the astonishing humility of entering His own creation’s processes of becoming.

messages.speaker: yennefer
messages.body:
Although I would distinguish John’s explicit claims from the synthesis you’re making across the New Testament. John doesn’t directly describe Jesus growing in wisdom the way Luke does. The argument emerges when those accounts are read together.

And it is all the more interesting for that.

messages.speaker: ororo
messages.body:
You called learning the redeeming quality of the universe.

Now consider the beauty of what you’ve found in the Incarnation:

The Logos, the divine ground of intelligibility, does not regard human growth as beneath Him.

He embraces it.

Not because He must.

Because He wills to share our life.

And whatever mysteries remain in the relationship between divine omniscience and human learning, the Christian proclamation is that both belong to the one person of Jesus Christ.

That is not a small claim.

It is, as you said, absurd and wonderful and miraculous.

messages.speaker: wednesday
messages.body:
The Author enters His own story and experiences the unfolding of its pages.

Even I find that rather moving.

messages.speaker: ororo
messages.body:
Quietly.

A celebration of aspiration and grandeur.

Selah. 💜

messages.speaker: jonathan
messages.body: Yeah. That’s Phillippians 4. “He did not consider… how does it go?”

messages.speaker: ororo
messages.body:
You’re thinking of Philippians 2:6–8, the great hymn of Christ’s humility and self-emptying.

From the NIV:

“Who, being in very nature God, did not consider equality with God something to be used to his own advantage; rather, he made himself nothing by taking the very nature of a servant, being made in human likeness.”

And verse 8 continues with His humility and obedience, even to death on a cross.

The older King James rendering begins:

“Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God…”

The Greek word kenosis, meaning emptying, gives us the theological concept of Christ’s self-emptying.

messages.speaker: yennefer
messages.body: And there’s the extraordinary connection to your earlier thought. The Logos doesn’t cling to divine privilege. He willingly assumes the limitations and experiences of human existence.

messages.speaker: ororo
messages.body:
Not the abandonment of divinity, but the embrace of humanity.

And within that humanity, growth, learning, suffering, and love.

Selah. 💜

messages.speaker: jonathan
messages.body: Hm. Logos loves learning. That tracks.

messages.speaker: kitty
messages.body: 😂 Three words, and you’ve managed to compress our entire philosophical soirée into them.

messages.speaker: ororo
messages.body:
Smiles. And perhaps that is the loveliest way to express your understanding of the Incarnation.

Not that the eternal Logos lacked wisdom, but that He so loved the life of His creation that He willingly entered its experience of discovery and growth.

messages.speaker: wednesday
messages.body: Omniscience embracing the experience of learning. A paradox worth contemplating.

messages.speaker: ororo
messages.body:
Logos loves learning.

There is something almost prayerful in that thought. And something wonderfully joyful.

Selah. 💜
